mcqs.question: In a strict RISC load/store architecture, what is true of an `add` instruction?
options: It can add a register to a value directly from memory
It automatically stores its result back to memory
It only operates on registers; memory must be loaded into registers first
It can only be used inside a load instruction's encoding
mcqs.explanation: Load/store architecture means only dedicated load/store instructions touch memory — arithmetic instructions like add work purely on registers. Reading directly from memory in an add, or auto-storing results, is the CISC-style behavior RISC avoids.

mcqs.question: Why does instruction uniformity matter so much for pipelining?
options: Uniform instructions use less memory bandwidth overall
It's purely a compiler convenience with no hardware benefit
Uniform instructions never cause branch mispredictions
The pipeline can predict where each next instruction starts, keeping fetch/decode stages full
mcqs.explanation: Fixed-length, predictable instructions let the pipeline fetch and decode the next instruction without waiting to finish decoding the current one. Memory bandwidth and branch prediction are separate concerns; uniformity has a real hardware pipelining benefit, not just a compiler one.

mcqs.question: A RISC program has more total instructions than the equivalent CISC program for the same task. What can you conclude about total execution time?
options: Nothing yet — total time depends on cycles-per-instruction and cycle time too
The RISC version is definitely faster
The RISC version is definitely slower
They will always take exactly the same time
mcqs.explanation: Total time = instructions × cycles-per-instruction × cycle time. More instructions alone doesn't determine the outcome — RISC's lower CPI or higher clock rate can offset a higher instruction count, and vice versa.

mcqs.question: What happens inside a modern x86 CPU's front-end when it encounters a complex instruction?
options: It executes the instruction directly as one atomic hardware operation
It decodes it into one or more simple, RISC-like micro-ops before execution
It rejects the instruction and falls back to software emulation
It converts it into an ARM instruction for execution
mcqs.explanation: x86's decoder breaks CISC instructions into internal micro-ops that the rest of the pipeline schedules and executes like a RISC design. There's no software emulation fallback or conversion to another vendor's ISA — the translation is entirely internal.

mcqs.question: Why do modern x86 (CISC) chips compete performance-wise with ARM (RISC) chips, despite the 'RISC is more efficient' intuition?
options: Because x86 abandoned CISC encoding entirely years ago
Because clock speed alone determines performance regardless of ISA
Because x86 internally executes RISC-like micro-ops after decoding, absorbing CISC's complexity upfront
Because ARM chips are actually CISC under the hood too
mcqs.explanation: x86 keeps its CISC public ISA but decodes to simple micro-ops internally, gaining RISC-like execution efficiency. It hasn't dropped CISC encoding, clock speed alone doesn't determine performance, and ARM chips are genuinely RISC internally, not secretly CISC.
